## 2. Homothetic Self-Similar Solutions

Let $U$ be a homothetic self-similar solution to the Navier-Stokes Equations. By definition there exists $\beta$ with $\beta\neq 1,0$ such that $U$ and $\beta U$ are both self-similar profiles; in particular, both solve Equation (2). Henceforth we shall always assume that any profile $U$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with $d\in\{2,3\}$ we analyze satisfies:

$$ U\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\qquad\lim_{R\to\infty}RU(R\cdot)=u_{0}(\cdot)\textrm{ in }\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). $$

This excludes pathological cases such as when harmonic gradients survive in the self-similar heat equation or the case of constant profiles. We thus work with any tempered distribution for which the natural blow-down limit exists. All the explicit examples we deal with here (such as the Okamoto shear flow) satisfy the condition in Equation (5). Then we have the following short lemma:

#### Lemma 2.1.

$U$ is a homothetic self-similar solution to the Navier-Stokes equations if and only if there exists a scalar pressure $P$ such that

$$ \begin{gathered}U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla P=0\\
\frac{U}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla U+\Delta U=0\\
\textrm{div }U=0.\end{gathered} $$

Moreover, if $U$ is homothetic, then $\beta U$ is a solution for all $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ .

#### Proof.

By hypothesis we know that there exists $P$ and $P_{\beta}$ such that

$$ -\frac{U}{2}-\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla U-\Delta U+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla P=0 $$

and

$$ -\beta\frac{U}{2}-\beta\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla U-\beta\Delta U+\beta^{2}U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla P_{\beta}=0. $$

Put $\mathcal{A}=\Delta+\tfrac{1}{2}(1+x\cdot\nabla)$ . Subtracting $\beta^{2}$ times the first equation from the second gives

$$ \mathcal{A}U=\nabla H,\qquad H=\frac{\beta^{2}P-P_{\beta}}{\beta^{2}-\beta},\qquad\Delta H=0. $$

By our assumption in Equation (5), we have that $U$ is a tempered distribution, so $AU$ is a tempered harmonic distribution and hence a polynomial, which we denote by $q$ . Set $U_{R}(x)=RU(Rx)$ . Then

$$ Rq(R\cdot)=R^{-2}\Delta U_{R}+\frac{1}{2}(U_{R}+x\cdot\nabla U_{R}). $$

By the assumption in Equation (5), the right-hand side converges in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ as $R\to\infty$ . No nonzero polynomial $q$ can have $Rq(R\cdot)$ converge in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ . Thus $AU=0$ , and the first equation gives $U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla P=0$ . Conversely these two identities imply that every $\beta U$ is a profile, with pressure $\beta^{2}P$ . ∎

Our first goal becomes one of constructing solutions of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-type equation (see [23] and [25] for work on similar systems)

$$ \begin{gathered}\frac{U}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla U+\Delta U=0\\
\textrm{div }u=0\end{gathered} $$

from $(-1)$ -homogeneous data $u_{0}(x)$ at infinity, in the sense that the following blow-down limit holds in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ :

$$ \lim_{R\to\infty}RU(R\cdot x)=u_{0}(x). $$

This corresponds to constructing forward self-similar solutions of the heat equation from $(-1)$ -homogeneous data at initial time. We therefore consider the following data:

$$ u_{0}(x)=|x|^{-1}\cdot v(\tfrac{x}{|x|}). $$

Our construction has two steps: from the data we first construct a distribution $a\colon\mathbb{S}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}^{3}$ which captures the angular information of the solution $U$ , then we construct $U$ from $a$ . What permits this route is the radial symmetry of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator. In our work below, the notation $n!!$ refers to the usual double factorial. The space $H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{S}^{2},\mathbb{C}^{3})$ is defined in terms of spherical harmonics $a_{kl}$ as the Hilbert space with the following norm

$$ \|a\|_{H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{S}^{2},\mathbb{C}^{3})}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=-l}^{k=l}(1+k(k+1))^{-1/2}|a_{kl}|^{2}. $$

We also recall that the Funk-Hecke formula (see [27]) for integration against a kernel on the sphere is

$$ \int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}K(\omega\cdot\Omega)Y_{kl}(\Omega)d\Omega=2\pi\left(\int_{-1}^{1}K(t)P_{k}(t)dt\right)Y_{kl}(\omega), $$

where $K$ is some kernel function, $P_{k}$ is the Legendre polynomial at order $k$ , and $Y_{kl}$ is the spherical harmonic at its respective order.

#### Lemma 2.2 (from $v$ to $a$ ).

Let $v\in L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{3})$ and let $Y_{kl}$ be the orthonormal spherical harmonics. Define $a=Tv$ harmonic-wise by the multipliers

$$ TY_{kl}=t_{k}Y_{kl},\qquad t_{k}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{(-1)^{(k-1)/2}}{4\pi i}\frac{k!!}{(k-1)!!},&k\text{ odd},\\[3.0pt]
\displaystyle\frac{(-1)^{k/2}}{2\pi^{2}}\frac{2^{k}((k/2)!)^{2}}{k!},&k\text{ even}.\end{cases} $$

Then $a\in H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{S}^{2};\mathbb{C}^{3})$ and $a(-\omega)=\overline{a(\omega)}$ . With $a_{\pm}(\omega)=(a(\omega)\pm a(-\omega))/2$ , the identity

$$ |x|^{-1}v(x/|x|)=\pi\langle a_{+}(\omega),\delta(\omega\cdot x)\rangle_{\omega}+i\left\langle a_{-}(\omega),\operatorname{PV}\frac{1}{\omega\cdot x}\right\rangle_{\omega} $$

holds in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ . These expressions mean that the kernel is first tested in $x$ against a Schwartz function, and only then paired with the distribution in $\omega$ .

#### Proof.

The factorial ratios and Stirling’s approximation give $|t_{k}|\leq C(1+k)^{1/2}$ . Hence, writing $v=\sum c_{kl}Y_{kl}$ , we see

$$ \sum_{k,l}(1+k(k+1))^{-1/2}|t_{k}c_{kl}|^{2}\leq C\sum_{k,l}|c_{kl}|^{2}, $$

which shows that $a\in H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ . The even multipliers are real and the odd multipliers are purely imaginary, which proves the symmetry $a(-\omega)=\overline{a(\omega)}$ that guarantees that $v$ is real. Now we prove the distributional identity.

For a finite harmonic sum, we apply the Funk-Hecke formula to the even kernel $\delta_{0}(t)$ and to the odd kernel $\textrm{P.V.}(1/t)$ . The following Legendre polynomial identities for $P_{2m}(0)$ and $\int_{-1}^{1}P_{2m+1}(t)/t\,dt$ are, respectively, from [10, formula (18.12.11)] with $x=0$ and [10, formula (18.17.39)] with $z=0$ , using parity:

$$ P_{2m}(0)=(-1)^{m}\frac{(2m)!}{2^{2m}(m!)^{2}},\qquad\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{P_{2m+1}(s)}{s}\,ds=2(-1)^{m}\frac{(2m)!!}{(2m+1)!!}. $$

These identities show that the harmonic-wise multipliers are exactly $t_{k}^{-1}$ . This proves the claimed distributional identity for finite sums. For Schwartz test functions in $x$ , testing either kernel produces a smooth function of $\omega$ : locally rotate $\omega$ to a fixed coordinate direction and differentiate the rotated Schwartz test function. Thus both kernel expressions depend continuously on $a$ as distributions. Partial sums of spherical harmonics converge to $v$ in $L^{2}$ and to $Tv$ in $H^{-1/2}$ . The homogeneous extensions from $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ converge in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ by polar coordinates and the rapid decay of the test function. Passing to the limit proves the identity for the stated data. ∎

#### Lemma 2.3 (From $a$ to $U$ ).

Let $a\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{S}^{2};\mathbb{C}^{3})$ satisfy $a(-\omega)=\overline{a(\omega)}$ . Define

$$ U(\xi)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\left\langle a(\omega),e^{-(\omega\cdot\xi)^{2}/4}\right\rangle+i\left\langle a(\omega),D(\omega\cdot\xi/2)\right\rangle,\quad D(z)=e^{-z^{2}}\int_{0}^{z}e^{t^{2}}\,dt. $$

Then $U\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3};\mathbb{R}^{3})$ and

$$ \Delta U+\frac{1}{2}\xi\cdot\nabla U+\frac{1}{2}U=0. $$

If $\omega\cdot a=0$ distributionally, then $\operatorname{div}U=0$ .

#### Proof.

The kernels depend smoothly on $(\xi,\omega)$ , so the distributional pairings therefore depend smoothly on $\xi$ , with derivatives obtained by differentiating the kernels. That $U$ is real follows by conjugation and the substitution $\omega\mapsto-\omega$ . Put $s=\omega\cdot\xi$ and let $K_{e}(s)=(\sqrt{\pi}/2)e^{-s^{2}/4}$ for the even kernel and $K_{o}(s)=iD(s/2)$ for the odd kernel. Direct differentiation gives

$$ K_{e}^{\prime\prime}+\frac{s}{2}K_{e}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{2}K_{e}=0,\qquad K_{o}^{\prime\prime}+\frac{s}{2}K_{o}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{2}K_{o}=0. $$

Since $|\omega|=1$ , these identities imply (9) after pairing with $a$ . Finally,

$$ \operatorname{div}U=\left\langle\omega\cdot a,K_{e}^{\prime}(\omega\cdot\xi)+K_{o}^{\prime}(\omega\cdot\xi)\right\rangle=0 $$

under the stated tangency hypothesis. ∎

Note that in fact any distribution $a$ with $a(\omega)\cdot\omega=0$ gives rise to a solution of Equation (7), but its convergence to the data may be less well-understood. Finally, we prove the following.

#### Proposition 2.4.

Let $v\in L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{3})$ and suppose $u_{0}(x)=|x|^{-1}v(x/|x|)$ is divergence free in $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ . Then $U=e^{\Delta}u_{0}$ is real, smooth, divergence free, and satisfies (7). It equals the profile obtained from $a=Tv$ in Lemmas 2.2 and 2.3. Moreover,

$$ U_{R}(x):=RU(Rx)=e^{R^{-2}\Delta}(u_{0}(x))\longrightarrow u_{0}(x) $$

in $L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ and in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ , and pointwise at every Lebesgue point of $u_{0}$ . If $v$ is continuous, this gives pointwise convergence at every $x\neq 0$ . The data uniquely determines every tempered solution of (7) with this distributional boundary value, by Lemma 2.5. If in addition $U$ is a stationary solution of the Euler equations, then $U$ is homothetic.

#### Proof.

Use of polar coordinates gives

$$ \int_{B_{R}}|u_{0}|^{2}=R\|v\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2})}^{2}. $$

Thus $u_{0}$ is locally square integrable and a tempered distribution. Convolution with the heat kernel is smooth and commutes with distributional divergence. Homogeneity and a change of variables give

$$ e^{t\Delta}u_{0}(x)=t^{-1/2}U(x/\sqrt{t}). $$

Differentiating this solution to the heat equation at $t=1$ proves (7), and the same identity gives (8). For completeness, we give a local approximate-identity argument that also applies at the origin. On a fixed ball $B_{M}$ , split $u_{0}$ by a smooth cutoff equal to one on $B_{2M}$ . The cutoff part is in $L^{2}$ , so convolution with the heat kernel tends to it in $L^{2}$ and at its Lebesgue points. For the remainder, $|x-y|\geq|y|/2$ when $x\in B_{M}$ , $|y|\geq 2M$ , so we have

$$ C\int_{|y|\geq 2M}t^{-1/2}e^{-|x-y|^{2}/(4t)}u_{0}(y)dy\leq C_{M,v}t^{-1/2}e^{-M^{2}/(4t)}. $$

The latter term tends to zero when $t\to 0$ . Convergence in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ follows from the Schwartz approximate-identity property. It remains to prove the distributional angular identity. In one dimension

$$ e^{\Delta}\delta(s)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}e^{-s^{2}/4},\qquad e^{\Delta}\operatorname{PV}(1/s)=D(s/2). $$

For the second identity, we first observe that the convolution $F=e^{\Delta}\operatorname{PV}(1/s)$ is odd and next that direct differentiation gives $F^{\prime}+sF/2=1/2$ . Finally, we know that the unique solution of this ODE with $F(0)=0$ is $D(s/2)$ . The same identities hold for kernels depending only on $s=\omega\cdot x$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . Apply convolution with the heat kernel to the distributional identity in Lemma 2.2. It commutes with the angular pairing after testing in $x$ , and yields precisely the kernels in Lemma 2.3. This also proves the divergence free property of the angular construction directly from the data. Uniqueness follows from Lemma 2.5. Finally, solving the stationary Euler equations together with $\mathcal{A}U=0$ implies that $U$ is a homothetic profile. ∎

#### Lemma 2.5.

Let $U\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ satisfy $\Delta U+\tfrac{1}{2}(U+x\cdot\nabla U)=0$ . If $RU(R\,\cdot)\to u_{0}$ in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ as $R\to\infty$ , then $U=e^{\Delta}u_{0}$ .

#### Proof.

Set $w(t,x)=t^{-1/2}U(x/\sqrt{t})$ . Then $\partial_{t}w=\Delta w$ and $w(t)\to u_{0}$ in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ . In Fourier space,

$$ \partial_{t}\bigl(e^{t|\xi|^{2}}\widehat{w}(t,\xi)\bigr)=0\quad\hbox{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). $$

The multiplier is used only against compactly supported frequency test functions. Taking $t\downarrow 0$ shows that this function that is constant in time must be precisely $\widehat{u}_{0}$ , so $\widehat{w}(t)=e^{-t|\xi|^{2}}\widehat{u}_{0}$ . Letting $t=1$ proves the claim. ∎

By the lemmas above, every homothetic profile satisfying the assumption in Equation (5) equals $e^{\Delta}u_{0}$ , where $u_{0}$ is its distributional blow-down limit. For angular $L^{2}$ data in dimension three, Proposition 2.4 therefore supplies the almost-everywhere convergence to $u_{0}$ required in the proof of Proposition 3.1.

#### Remark 2.6.

Let us point out that the boundary condition in [17] and [18] given by

$$ |U(x)-u_{0}(x)|=o(|x|^{-1})\qquad\text{ as }|x|\to+\infty $$

implies that $u_{0}$ is the blow-down limit of $U$ .

## 3. Properties of Homothetic Solutions

### 3.1. Regularity of the Data

In this subsection, we shall prove Theorem 1.1. For $1\leq q\leq p$ , our convention is that $f\in\mathcal{M}_{q}^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ if and only if there is $C<\infty$ such that

$$ \int_{B_{r}(x)}|f|^{q}\leq Cr^{3-3q/p}\quad\hbox{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^{3},\ r>0. $$

The following result states explicitly the convergence used to pass to the Euler equation. For homothetic profiles with angular $L^{2}$ data, that convergence is supplied by Proposition 2.4.

#### Proposition 3.1.

Let $U$ be a homothetic profile on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and suppose $U\in\mathcal{M}_{q}^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ for some $2<q\leq 3$ . Assume additionally that $U_{R}(x)=RU(Rx)$ converges almost everywhere to a measurable vector field $u_{0}$ as $R\to\infty$ . Then $u_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{q}^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ is homogeneous of degree $-1$ and is a divergence-free weak stationary Euler field on all of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . The convergence also holds in $L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ and in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ .

#### Proof.

The critical Morrey estimate is invariant under this scaling:

$$ \int_{B_{r}(x)}|U_{R}|^{q}=R^{q-3}\int_{B_{Rr}(Rx)}|U|^{q}\leq Cr^{3-q}. $$

Fatou’s lemma gives the identical bound for $u_{0}$ . On each compact set $K$ , Hölder’s inequality gives

$$ \int_{E}|U_{R}|^{2}\leq C_{K}|E|^{1-2/q},\qquad E\subset K, $$

uniformly in $R$ . Since $q>2$ , this proves uniform integrability of the family $|U_{R}|^{2}$ . An alternate proof of the uniform integrability uses the Morrey condition and the theorem of De Le Vallée Poussin (cf. [4]). By the assumed pointwise convergence and Vitali’s theorem (see [5]), $U_{R}\to u_{0}$ strongly in $L^{2}(K)$ . In particular,

$$ \displaystyle\|U_{R}\otimes U_{R}-u_{0}\otimes u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(K)} \displaystyle\leq(\|U_{R}\|_{L^{2}(K)}+\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}(K)})\|U_{R}-u_{0}\|_{L^{2}(K)}\longrightarrow 0. $$

Since $U$ is homothetic, $U$ solves the stationary Euler equations, so every $U_{R}$ solves the stationary Euler equations. For every $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3};\mathbb{R}^{3})$ with $\operatorname{div}\phi=0$ , the preceding limit gives $\int(u_{0}\otimes u_{0}):\nabla\phi=0$ . The divergence free property passes to the limit as well. The Morrey estimate also gives $\int_{B_{r}}|U_{R}|\leq Cr^{2}$ uniformly in $R$ and the same holds for $u_{0}$ . Splitting a Schwartz test function into a compactly supported part and into dyadic annuli improves the local convergence to convergence in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ by a standard argument. Finally $U_{R}(\lambda x)=\lambda^{-1}U_{\lambda R}(x)$ for $\lambda>0$ . Passing to the distributional limit proves $u_{0}(\lambda x)=\lambda^{-1}u_{0}(x)$ , thus the $(-1)$ -homogeneity of $u_{0}$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.2.

Writing $u_{0}(r\omega)=r^{-1}v(\omega)$ , its local $L^{q}$ membership on an annulus $\{x:1<|x|<2\}$ gives $v\in L^{q}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ . At $q=3$ , the Morrey convention above gives $\mathcal{M}_{3}^{3}=L^{3}$ . Note that a nonzero homogeneous data of degree $-1$ cannot lie in this space because its radial integral contains $\int_{0}^{\infty}dr/r$ . Nonzero homogeneous data only makes sense when $q<3$ .

#### Remark 3.3.

Note that the choice of Morrey space we make is not quite arbitrary. For instance, Taylor and Kato prove in [29] and respectively [19] that the Morrey space $\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ admits a small-data global well-posedness result for mild solutions whenever $q\in(1,3]$ . Of course, any solution satisfying the boundary conditions of Jia and Šverák trivially belongs in this class as well.

#### 3.1.1. Three-Dimensions

In this subsection we prove Theorem 1.1, which is a conditional Liouville theorem for homothetic self-similar solutions. The main idea of the proof is to instead show that the data (a $(-1)$ -homogeneous solution to the Euler equations) is trivial by sharpening a similar proof from [28]. We split the proof of Theorem 1.1 into two propositions, each of which handles one itemized hypothesis from the statement of Theorem 1.1. We begin with:

#### Proposition 3.4.

Suppose $U$ is a homothetic forward self-similar solution to the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations lying in the Morrey space $\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ for some $2<q\leq 3$ . Suppose that the forward self-similar solution corresponds to initial data

$$ u_{0}=\frac{\vec{v}+f\vec{n}}{|x|}\in L^{q}(\mathbb{S}^{2}), $$

where $\vec{n}$ is the unit normal to the sphere and $\vec{v}$ is a tangent vector field to the sphere. Suppose $\vec{v}\in W^{1,4/3}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ and $f\in L^{4}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ . Then $f=0$ and the head pressure $|\vec{v}|^{2}+2p=0$ as well. If, in addition, the set $\{\omega\in\mathbb{S}^{2}:\vec{v}(\omega)=0\}$ has measure zero or is a closed set with $C^{2}$ boundary, then $\vec{v}=u_{0}=U=0$ .

#### Proof.

We know by Proposition 3.1 that $u_{0}$ is a stationary solution of the three-dimensional Euler equations. This reduces to a system of differential equations on the sphere:

$$ \begin{cases}(\nabla^{\perp}\cdot v)v^{\perp}+\nabla\left(\frac{1}{2}|v|^{2}+p\right)=0\\
v\cdot\nabla f=|v|^{2}+f^{2}+2p\\
f+\nabla\cdot v=0.\end{cases} $$

Here we have abused notation by writing $v$ instead of $\vec{v}$ . We remark that the first equation in the system above can be written as

$$ v\cdot\nabla v+\nabla p=0, $$

therefore we can always recover the pressure from

$$ -\Delta p=\textrm{div}^{2}(v\otimes v)+|v|^{2}+2p. $$

Since $v\in W^{1,4/3}\subset L^{4}$ , it follows from standard elliptic regularity that $p\in L^{2}$ . Let $h:=2p+|v|^{2}\in L^{2}$ . Then we have that $h,f$ satisfy the following transport equations:

$$ v\cdot\nabla h=0 $$

and

$$ v\cdot\nabla f=h+f^{2}. $$

Since $v\in L^{4},f\in L^{4}$ , and $h\in L^{2}$ , we have that $vfh\in L^{1}$ , and in particular, $vfh$ is a distribution (i.e. we can take its divergence). Since $v\in W^{1,4/3}$ , we can say that the following integrals are justified

$$ 0=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}\textrm{div }(vfh)=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}(\nabla\cdot v)fh+\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}h(v\cdot\nabla f)+\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}f(v\cdot\nabla h)=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}h^{2}. $$

From here we conclude that $h\equiv 0$ , which, along with $v\in W^{1,4/3}$ , implies that the distribution $(\nabla^{\perp}\cdot v)v^{\perp}=0$ . Now since $v\in L^{4}$ and $f^{3}\in L^{4/3}$ , we get $vf^{3}\in L^{1}$ and the following integrals are justified:

$$ 0=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}\textrm{div}(vf^{3})=2\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}f^{4}. $$

We conclude that $f\equiv 0$ , which implies that $\nabla\cdot v=0$ . This concludes the proof that $u_{0}$ must be tangential to the sphere, divergence free, and with zero head pressure whenever $u_{0}$ lies in this regularity class. If in addition, $v$ has a Lebesgue null zero set, then we have to conclude $\nabla^{\perp}\cdot v=0$ a.e., so $v$ is harmonic and therefore zero on $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ . Otherwise, if the boundary of the (closed) null set of $v$ is $C^{2}$ , then whenever $v$ is not zero, it is harmonic (on a $C^{2}$ open subset of $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ ). Therefore, $v=0$ necessarily on that set as well. ∎

#### Remark 3.5.

In the proof above, there remains a pathological case: that the data $u_{0}=\vec{v}/|x|$ is a distributionally divergence-free vector field that has $\vec{v}=0$ on a rough non-null set $Z$ and that $\textrm{curl }_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}\vec{v}=0$ in the distributional sense on the complement of $Z$ in $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ . In the context of our Liouville theorem, this is an issue of the method of proof rather than a real obstruction to a rigidity result. In our forthcoming work, we bypass any such obstacle and prove rigidity of homothetic solutions for spherical data $u_{0}\in L^{q}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ for any $q>2$ , which certainly subsumes the case discussed above regardless of the behavior of the support.

#### Remark 3.6.

Instead of assumptions on the null set of $\vec{v}$ , we may assume continuity of $\vec{v}$ to conclude the conditional Liouville theorem. For instance, if $v\in W^{1,q}$ with $q>2$ , then $v$ is continuous. Then we get $(\nabla^{\perp}\cdot v)|v^{\perp}|^{2}=0$ a.e. on $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ . Since $v$ is continuous, we conclude that the $L^{q}$ function $\nabla^{\perp}\cdot v=0$ a.e. on the open set $\{x\in\mathbb{S}^{2}:|v(x)|\neq 0\}$ . In addition, $\nabla^{\perp}\cdot v=0$ trivially on the interior of the zero set $\{x\in\mathbb{S}^{2}:|v(x)|=0\}$ . We conclude that $\nabla^{\perp}\cdot v=0$ a.e. on $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ . Combined with the knowledge that $\nabla\cdot v=0$ on $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ , we know that $\Delta v=0$ a.e. on $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ . This implies that $v=0$ .

We now prove the other part of Theorem 1.1:

#### Proposition 3.7.

Suppose $U$ is a homothetic forward self-similar solution to the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations lying in the Morrey space $\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ for some $2<q\leq 3$ . Suppose that the forward self-similar solution corresponds to initial data

$$ u_{0}=\frac{\vec{v}+f\vec{n}}{|x|}\in L^{q}(\mathbb{S}^{2}), $$

where $\vec{n}$ is the unit normal to the sphere and $\vec{v}$ is a tangent vector field to the sphere. Suppose $\vec{v},f\in C^{\alpha}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ , for some $\alpha>1/2$ . Then $f=\vec{v}=u_{0}=U=0$ .

#### Proof.

Note that since $\alpha>1/2$ , the product $v\cdot\nabla q$ makes sense as a distribution in $B^{\alpha-1}_{\infty,\infty}$ for any $q\in C^{\alpha}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ . We let $|v|^{2}+f^{2}+2p:=H$ .

For any vector field or function $q$ on the sphere, we consider its mollification $q_{\epsilon}$ . Following the idea from [9], we have the following commutator estimate for any $q\in C^{\alpha}$ .

$$ \|(v_{\epsilon}\cdot\nabla q_{\epsilon})-(v\cdot\nabla q)_{\epsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\epsilon^{2\alpha-1}\|q\|_{C^{\alpha}}\|v\|_{C^{\alpha}}. $$

Therefore, for every $\alpha>1/2$ , we have:

$$ v_{\epsilon}\cdot\nabla f_{\epsilon}=H_{\epsilon}+R_{1}(\epsilon), $$

and

$$ v_{\epsilon}\cdot\nabla h_{\epsilon}=R_{2}(\epsilon), $$

where $R_{i}(\epsilon)\to 0$ as $\epsilon\to 0$ . Performing an integration by parts as in the proof of the nonexistence of $(-1)$ -homogeneous Euler solutions in the $C^{1}$ category (see [28] or consider $\textrm{div }(f_{\epsilon}v_{\epsilon}h_{\epsilon})$ ) and taking $\epsilon\to 0$ implies that $f=H=0$ and moreover:

$$ (\textrm{curl }v)v^{\perp}=0, $$

in the distributional sense (note that the product makes sense as a distribution in $B^{\alpha-1}_{\infty,\infty}$ ). Since $v$ is continuous, the set $U$ that is the complement in $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ of the zero set of $v$ is an open set. What we get from the above equality is that $\textrm{curl }v=0$ on $U$ in the distributional sense. Since $\textrm{div }v=0$ on $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ , we conclude that $v$ is a distributionally harmonic vector field on $U$ . In particular, $v$ is smooth on $U$ and is a classically harmonic vector field on $U$ . However, we have already that $v=0$ on the complement of $U$ . This yields that $v=0$ on $\mathbb{S}^{2}$ . ∎

#### 3.1.2. Two-Dimensions

The following result classifies homothetic profiles with continuous angular Euler data and a distributional blow-down limit.

#### Proposition 3.8.

Suppose $U$ is a homothetic forward self-similar solution to the two-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations and $RU(R\,\cdot)\to u_{0}=b(\omega)/r$ in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , where $b\in C(\mathbb{S}^{1};\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Suppose $\operatorname{div}u_{0}=0$ in $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and that $u_{0}$ solves the stationary Euler equations distributionally on $\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus\{0\}$ . Then we necessarily have

$$ b(\omega)=A\omega^{\perp}, $$

where $\omega=(\cos(\theta),\sin(\theta))$ , in polar coordinates. In particular, $U$ is necessarily the Oseen vortex:

$$ U(r,\omega)=A\frac{1-e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{4}}}{r}\omega^{\perp}. $$

#### Proof.

Write $b=fe_{r}+ge_{\theta}$ . Incompressibility gives $g=c$ constant, and incompressibility across the origin requires $\int_{0}^{2\pi}f\,d\theta=0$ . The momentum equation has zero tangential component and radial component $r^{-3}(cf^{\prime}-f^{2}-c^{2})+\partial_{r}P_{0}=0$ . Hence $P_{0}$ is radial and, for a real constant $K$ ,

$$ cf^{\prime}=f^{2}+c^{2}-K. $$

If $c\neq 0$ , continuity gives $f\in C^{1}$ ; multiplying by $f^{\prime}$ and integrating over one period gives $c\int_{0}^{2\pi}(f^{\prime})^{2}\,d\theta=0$ , so $f$ is constant. If $c=0$ , the identity $f^{2}=K$ and continuity on the circle again make $f$ constant. Its zero mean forces $f=0$ . Thus $u_{0}=Ae_{\theta}/r$ with $A=c$ .

Lemma 2.5 gives $U=e^{\Delta}u_{0}$ . Since $\operatorname{curl}u_{0}=2\pi A\delta_{0}$ , $\operatorname{curl}U=(A/2)e^{-r^{2}/4}$ . The heat convolution is smooth, divergence free, and rotation invariant, so its radial component vanishes. Integrating $(rU_{\theta})^{\prime}=(A/2)re^{-r^{2}/4}$ from zero gives

$$ U(r,\omega)=A\frac{1-e^{-r^{2}/4}}{r}\,\omega^{\perp}. $$

∎

#### Remark 3.9.

If $u_{0}(r,\omega)=\frac{\omega^{\perp}}{r}$ exhibits non-uniqueness, then the other forward self-similar solution cannot be homothetic.

#### Remark 3.10.

Note that the case of $(-1)$ -homogeneous steady states of Euler on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ corresponds to the point vortex solutions, so these cannot correspond to classical distributional solutions in the whole domain $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ .

#### Remark 3.11.

The $(-1)$ -homogeneous shear flow

$$ \overline{U}_{1,\beta}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})=\left(\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}e^{-\frac{\xi_{2}^{2}}{4}}\text{erfi}\left(\frac{\xi_{2}}{2}\right),0\right) $$

with boundary data $(\mathrm{P.V.}(1/y),0)$ , is not ruled out by this theorem since the angular data is far from being in $L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{1})$ .

### 3.2. Regularity to Decay Relationship

This subsection makes the relationship between the regularity of the spherical data (in Fourier space or in physical space) and the decay of the resulting profile a bit clearer. Consider a profile constructed from an angular distribution $a$ by Lemma 2.3. Write

$$ \displaystyle U_{\mathrm{even}}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\left\langle a(\omega),e^{-(\omega\cdot x)^{2}/4}\right\rangle_{\omega}, \displaystyle U_{\mathrm{odd}}(x) \displaystyle=i\langle a(\omega),D(\omega\cdot x/2)\rangle_{\omega},\qquad U=U_{\mathrm{even}}+U_{\mathrm{odd}}, $$

for the even and odd parts of the profile, respectively. We have the following elementary lemma:

#### Lemma 3.12.

For every unit vector $\eta$ and every $s>0$ ,

$$ \int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}e^{-s^{2}(\omega\cdot\eta)^{2}/4}\,d\omega=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}e^{-s^{2}t^{2}/4}\,dt\leq\frac{4\pi^{3/2}}{s}. $$

#### Proof.

Rotate $\eta$ to the point $(0,0,1)$ , so we get an integral over a great circle. Then if we parameterize the great circle appropriately and let $t=\cos\theta$ , we get the first equality. The inequality follows by extending the last integral to $\mathbb{R}$ and evaluating its Gaussian integral. ∎

The following proposition is further evidence for our heuristic that the regularity of the spherical data is directly related to the decay of the profile. It shows that bounded Fourier spherical data guarantees an isotropic profile.

#### Proposition 3.13.

Suppose $a\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2};\mathbb{C}^{3})$ in (12). Then

$$ \sup_{\eta\in\mathbb{S}^{2}}|U_{\mathrm{even}}(s\eta)|\leq\frac{2\pi^{2}}{s}\|a\|_{L^{\infty}},\qquad s>0. $$

In particular, if $a$ is real and even, the resulting profile has isotropic $O(|x|^{-1})$ decay. If it is also tangent to the sphere, the profile is divergence free. It is homothetic provided it additionally satisfies the stationary Euler equations.

#### Proof.

Take the absolute value in the even integral and apply Lemma 3.12. For real even $a$ the odd integral vanishes. Tangency implies the divergence free condition by Lemma 2.3. That lemma also gives $\mathcal{A}U=0$ , so solving the stationary Euler equations implies that $U$ is a homothetic profile. ∎

## 4. Examples of Homothetic Solutions

### 4.1. Atomic Measures

Every pair of Dirac masses supported at antipodal points $\pm\omega_{0}\in\mathbb{S}^{2}$ corresponds to what we term an Okamoto shear flow.

Let $\omega_{0}\in S^{2}$ and let $\omega_{1}\in S^{2}$ be orthogonal to $\omega_{0}$ (in particular $\omega_{1}$ lies on the great circle $G_{\omega_{0}}$ ). Consider the distribution

$$ a(\omega)=(\delta_{\omega_{0}}(\omega)+\delta_{-\omega_{0}}(\omega))\omega_{1}. $$

Evidently, this distribution satisfies the symmetry and divergence-free conditions we require on $a(\omega)$ , in particular $a(-\omega)=\overline{a(\omega)}$ and $\omega\cdot a(\omega)=0$ . Also, it is clear that this is an even distribution, i.e. $a(-\omega)=a(\omega)$ . Therefore, the corresponding solution to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck equation is, according to Equation (12) and up to constant prefactor,

$$ U(r,\omega)=\int_{S^{2}}e^{-\frac{(\omega\cdot\Omega)^{2}r^{2}}{4}}a(\Omega)d\Omega=\int_{S^{2}}e^{-\frac{(\omega\cdot\Omega)^{2}r^{2}}{4}}\left((\delta_{\omega_{0}}(\Omega)+\delta_{-\omega_{0}}(\Omega))\omega_{1}\right)d\Omega. $$

Therefore, up to an unimportant constant prefactor:

$$ U(r,\omega)=\omega_{1}e^{-\frac{(\omega\cdot\omega_{0})^{2}r^{2}}{4}}. $$

To illustrate this example more clearly, let $\omega_{0}=(0,1,0)$ and let, for instance $\omega_{1}=(1,0,0)$ . Then we can say:

$$ U(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\left(e^{-\xi_{2}^{2}/4},0,0\right). $$

This solution corresponds to a forward self-similar solution of Navier-Stokes from vortex sheet initial data $(\delta_{0}(y),0,0)$ , which lies in $BMO^{-1}$ , and was described by Okamoto in [26].

The other one-dimensional shear flow described by Okamoto comes from the distribution

$$ a(\omega)=-i\left(\delta_{\omega_{0}}(\omega)-\delta_{-\omega_{0}}(\omega)\right)\omega_{1}. $$

Indeed, in this case the distribution satisfies the symmetry and divergence-free conditions and is odd, so we only see the odd part:

$$ U(r,\omega)=\int_{S^{2}}D\left(\frac{r(\omega\cdot\Omega)}{2}\right)\left(\delta_{\omega_{0}}(\Omega)-\delta_{-\omega_{0}}(\Omega)\right)\omega_{1}d\Omega. $$

Therefore, up to an unimportant constant prefactor:

$$ U(r,\omega)=\omega_{1}D\left(\frac{r(\omega\cdot\omega_{0})}{2}\right). $$

To illustrate this example more clearly, let $\omega_{0}=(0,1,0)$ and $\omega_{1}=(1,0,0)$ , then we can say:

$$ U(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\left(D(\xi_{2}/2),0,0\right), $$

which is the other shear flow found by Okamoto. We also recognize this as the shear flow for which we shall later prove instability as promised in Theorem 1.3 of the introduction.

Formally, an Okamoto shear flow is of the form:

$$ S(\xi)=\omega_{1}F(\xi\cdot\omega_{0}), $$

where $\omega_{1}\perp\omega_{0}$ and $F$ is either the Gaussian or Dawson function. As done with the Mikado flow building blocks of convex integration, it is clear that the sum of any two Okamoto shear flows $S(\xi)$ and $S^{\prime}(\xi)$ with direction $\omega_{1}^{\prime}$ and decay in $\omega_{0}^{\prime}$ direction remains a homothetic self-similar solution if and only if

$$ \omega_{1}\cdot\omega_{0}^{\prime}=0\textrm{ and }\omega_{1}^{\prime}\cdot\omega_{0}=0, $$

which, in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , already forces at least one pair of directions to be parallel.

### 4.2. Measures Supported on Curves

Now we recover another example of Okamoto’s. Let $\omega_{0}\in S^{2}$ be arbitrary, and consider the great circle $G_{\omega_{0}}$ of vectors in $S^{2}$ orthogonal to $\omega_{0}$ . Consider the following vector valued measure supported on the great circle $G_{\omega_{0}}$

$$ a(\omega)=\delta_{0}(\omega\cdot\omega_{0})\omega_{0}. $$

This distribution is even, so we get

$$ U(r,\omega)=\int_{S^{2}}e^{-\frac{(\omega\cdot\Omega)^{2}r^{2}}{4}}\delta_{0}(\Omega\cdot\omega_{0})\omega_{0}d\Omega. $$

For illustrative purposes, let $\omega_{0}=(1,0,0)$ . The integral above now becomes an integral over the great circle $\gamma:=G_{\omega_{0}}$ , which we may parametrize by $\gamma(t)=(0,\cos(t),\sin(t))$ . We get:

$$ U(r,\omega)=(1,0,0)\int_{0}^{2\pi}e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{4}(\omega_{2}\cos(t)+\omega_{3}\sin(t))^{2}}dt. $$

However we note that up to unimportant prefactors:

$$ \int_{0}^{2\pi}\exp\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{4}(\omega_{2}\cos t+\omega_{3}\sin t)^{2}\right)dt= $$

$$ =\exp\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{8}(\omega_{2}^{2}+\omega_{3}^{2})\right)I_{0}\left(\frac{r^{2}}{8}(\omega_{2}^{2}+\omega_{3}^{2})\right), $$

where $I_{0}$ denotes the modified Bessel function of the first kind.

In cylindrical coordinates with axis parallel to $\omega_{0}=(1,0,0)$ , we have

$$ U(x_{1},\rho,\theta)=\left(e^{-\rho^{2}/8}I_{0}(\rho^{2}/8),0,0\right), $$

which is an axisymmetric shear flow identified by Okamoto in [26].

Our next particular solution shows that if $a(\omega)$ has the same support but a different vector field along the support, the corresponding homothetic solution can be quite different. Indeed, let $\omega_{0}\in S^{2}$ be arbitrary, and consider the great circle $G_{\omega_{0}}$ of vectors in $S^{2}$ orthogonal to $\omega_{0}$ . Consider the distribution supported on the great circle $G_{\omega_{0}}$ .

$$ a(\omega)=-i\delta_{0}(\omega\cdot\omega_{0})(\omega\times\omega_{0}). $$

This is an odd distribution that respects the symmetry condition to recover a real-valued vector field. In particular, because $a$ is odd we have

$$ U(r,\omega)=\int_{S^{2}}D\left(\frac{r(\omega\cdot\Omega)}{2}\right)\left(\delta_{0}(\Omega\cdot\omega_{0})(\Omega\times\omega_{0})\right)d\Omega. $$

Once again, this is simply an integral over the circle $G_{\omega_{0}}$ , which we parametrize by $(0,\cos(t),\sin(t))$ . The resulting integral is

$$ U(r,\omega)=\int_{0}^{2\pi}D\left(\frac{r}{2}(\omega_{2}\cos(t)+\omega_{3}\sin(t))\right)(0,\sin(t),-\cos(t))dt. $$

We can evaluate the integral and get, up to unimportant prefactors:

$$ U(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\frac{1-e^{-(\xi_{2}^{2}+\xi_{3}^{2})/4}}{\xi_{2}^{2}+\xi_{3}^{2}}\left(0,-\xi_{3},\xi_{2}\right). $$

In cylindrical coordinates, we see that

$$ U(x_{1},\rho,\theta)=\frac{1-e^{-\rho^{2}/4}}{\rho}e_{\theta}, $$

which is a pure swirl vector field. Essentially, this flow is the Oseen vortex lifted to three dimensions. We leave open the question whether another vector field distribution on the great circle can lead to a homothetic self-similar solution.

The Okamoto shear flow can be modified in the following way. Instead of having a distribution with support on the entire great circle, we allow the distribution to be supported on antipodal partial arcs of the great circle. If one expands the analytic integrand as a series and integrates term-by-term, one can find a series representation for the solutions in this case.

First we consider the distribution

$$ a(\omega)=\delta_{0}(\omega\cdot\omega_{0})\omega_{0}(\chi_{A}(\omega)+\chi_{-A}(\omega)), $$

where $\omega_{0}\in S^{2}$ is fixed and $A$ is some fixed subarc of the great circle $G_{\omega_{0}}$ that is disjoint from $-A$ . This remains an even, real-valued distribution and has the symmetry property $a(\omega)=\overline{a(-\omega)}$ . Since the distribution is even, we get

$$ U(r,\omega)=\int_{S^{2}}e^{-\frac{(\omega\cdot\Omega)^{2}r^{2}}{4}}\delta_{0}(\Omega\cdot\omega_{0})\omega_{0}(\chi_{A}(\Omega)+\chi_{-A}(\Omega))d\Omega. $$

For illustrative purposes, let $\omega_{0}=(1,0,0)$ . The integral above becomes an integral over the subarcs of the circle $\gamma:=G_{\omega_{0}}$ corresponding to $A$ and $-A$ , and we may parametrize the curve $\gamma$ by $\gamma(t)=(0,\cos(t),\sin(t))$ . Suppose the subarcs are exactly: $[\theta_{1},\theta_{2}]$ and $[\pi+\theta_{1},\pi+\theta_{2}]$ . We get:

$$ U(r,\omega)= $$

$$ =(1,0,0)\bigg(\int_{\theta_{1}}^{\theta_{2}}e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{4}(\omega_{2}\cos(t)+\omega_{3}\sin(t))^{2}}dt+ $$

$$ +\int_{\theta_{1}+\pi}^{\theta_{2}+\pi}e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{4}(\omega_{2}\cos(t)+\omega_{3}\sin(t))^{2}}dt\bigg). $$

Now let $\phi$ be the angle such that

$$ \cos(\phi)=\frac{\omega_{2}}{\sqrt{\omega_{2}^{2}+\omega_{3}^{2}}},\quad\sin(\phi)=\frac{\omega_{3}}{\sqrt{\omega_{2}^{2}+\omega_{3}^{2}}}. $$

In addition, let $\rho=\sqrt{x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2}}$ . Then:

$$ U(r,\omega)=(1,0,0)\left(2e^{-\rho^{2}/8}\int_{\theta_{1}-\phi}^{\theta_{2}-\phi}e^{-\frac{\rho^{2}}{8}\cos(2t)}dt\right). $$

We use the series expansion for $e^{-z}$ at $z=0$ :

$$ e^{-z}=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!}z^{n}. $$

Therefore, we may integrate term by term and get

$$ U(r,\omega)=(2,0,0)e^{-\rho^{2}/8}\sum_{n\geq 0}\int_{\theta_{1}-\phi}^{\theta_{2}-\phi}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!}\left(\frac{\rho^{2}}{8}\cos(2t)\right)^{n}dt, $$

or

$$ U(r,\omega)=(2,0,0)e^{-\rho^{2}/8}\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!}\left(\frac{\rho^{2}}{8}\right)^{n}\int_{\theta_{1}-\phi}^{\theta_{2}-\phi}\cos^{n}(2t)dt. $$

We observe that the solution $U$ we construct is no longer axisymmetric, unless $\theta_{2}-\theta_{1}=\pi$ or $2\pi$ , for which the integral above becomes independent of the angular variable and the solution reduces to a constant multiple of the previously discussed Okamoto shear flow. We also remark that since the profile above remains a shear flow, it is clearly a stationary solution of the three-dimensional Euler equations and therefore a homothetic solution. Let us compute the corresponding “data at infinity” by returning to the following general form of the profile:

$$ U(r,\omega)=(1,0,0)\left(2\int_{\theta_{1}-\phi}^{\theta_{2}-\phi}e^{-\frac{\rho^{2}}{4}\cos^{2}(t)}dt\right). $$

Therefore, $RU(Rr,\omega)$ is

$$ RU(Rr,\omega)=(1,0,0)\left(2R\int_{\theta_{1}-\phi}^{\theta_{2}-\phi}e^{-R^{2}\frac{\rho^{2}}{4}\cos^{2}(t)}dt\right). $$

As $R\to\infty$ , we see that the integral only contributes something nontrivial in the limit if $\cos(t)=0$ somewhere in the interval $[\theta_{1}-\phi,\theta_{2}-\phi]$ . Let $t_{k}$ be the roots of $\cos(t)$ in the interval, and let $N(\phi)$ be the number of roots in the interval. Then we have for some arbitrary $\epsilon>0$ :

$$ R\int_{\theta_{1}-\phi}^{\theta_{2}-\phi}e^{\tfrac{-(R\rho)^{2}}{4}\cos^{2}(t)}dt=R\int_{K}e^{\tfrac{-(R\rho)^{2}}{4}\cos^{2}(t)}dt+ $$

$$ \sum_{t_{k}\in[\theta_{1}-\phi,\theta_{2}-\phi]}R\int_{t_{k}-\epsilon}^{t_{k}+\epsilon}e^{\tfrac{-(R\rho)^{2}}{4}\cos^{2}(t)}dt. $$

Here we denoted $K$ to be the (compact) complement of the union of intervals $(t_{k}-\epsilon,t_{k}+\epsilon)$ relative to the original interval depending on $\phi$ . Since $\cos(t)$ does not vanish on $K$ , as $R\to\infty$ , the corresponding integral vanishes. For each term in the sum we have approximately:

$$ \lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{R\rho}{\rho}\int_{t_{k}-\epsilon}^{t_{k}+\epsilon}e^{-\frac{(R\rho)^{2}}{4}\cos^{2}(t)}dt\approx\lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{R\rho/2}{\rho/2}\int_{t_{k}-\epsilon}^{t_{k}+\epsilon}e^{-\frac{(R\rho)^{2}}{4}(t-t_{k})^{2}}dt= $$

$$ =\frac{2}{\rho}\lim_{M\to\infty}M\int_{t_{k}-\epsilon}^{t_{k}+\epsilon}e^{-M^{2}(t-t_{k})^{2}}dt=\frac{2}{\rho}\lim_{M\to\infty}\sqrt{\pi}\textrm{Erf}(M\epsilon)=\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}}{\rho}. $$

Therefore, up to an unimportant prefactor, we see that the data at infinity should be

$$ u_{0}(\rho,\phi,x_{1})=\frac{N(\phi)}{\rho}. $$

For illustrative purposes, if $\theta_{1}=\pi/2$ and $\theta_{2}=\pi$ as in our explicit example from before, then $N(\phi)$ is a step function:

$$ N(\phi):=\begin{cases}1,\textrm{ when }\phi\in[0,\pi/2]\cup[\pi,3\pi/2]\\
0,\textrm{ when }\phi\in(\pi/2,\pi)\cup(3\pi/2,2\pi).\end{cases} $$

Note how the data corresponds to the support of the measure we began the analysis with.

The case just discussed, when the measure is supported on a curve, gets us a profile whose blow-down limit is essentially $1/\rho$ , which fails to be in $L^{2}_{loc}$ (and therefore cannot be a weak solution to the Euler equations in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ ). This does not contradict our Proposition 3.1, since that result required that the homothetic solution lie in the Morrey space $\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}$ with $q>2$ , while the profiles constructed above lie in $\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}$ with $q<2$ . Nevertheless, we know that small-data global well-posedness results have been proven in the class $\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}$ for any $q>1$ , so the question of uniqueness from the simple data $\beta/\rho$ for large $\beta$ remains open and interesting.

Modifying the support of the vector-valued measure for the lifted Oseen profile in a similar way leads to a different outcome. The profile remains a solution of the self-similar heat equation and remains divergence free, but we are not guaranteed to obtain a profile that solves the stationary Euler equations (e.g. it does not have a shear flow structure). The question of what other vector valued measures would lead to homothetic solutions remains open and, in our view, is quite interesting.

### 4.3. Instability

Set $P(y)=D(y/2)$ where $D(z)$ is again the Dawson function. Set $\overline{U}_{\beta}(x)=\beta P(x_{2})e_{1}$ . We first construct an unstable mode via Rayleigh’s equation and an argument of Lin (from [21]), then we obtain approximate spectrum for the linearization of the three-dimensional Euler equations in velocity form on $L^{2}$ by constructing a wave packet along the lines suggested by the authors of [14].

#### Lemma 4.1.

Let $K=-P^{\prime\prime}/P$ , with its value at zero defined by continuity, and let $H=-d^{2}/dy^{2}-K$ on $H^{2}(\mathbb{R})\subset L^{2}(\mathbb{R})$ . Then $H$ has exactly one negative eigenvalue $-\alpha_{0}^{2}$ . For every $0<\alpha<\alpha_{0}$ there are $\gamma_{\alpha}>0$ and $0\neq\phi_{\alpha}\in H^{2}(\mathbb{R})$ such that

$$ (P-i\gamma_{\alpha})(\phi_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}-\alpha^{2}\phi_{\alpha})-P^{\prime\prime}\phi_{\alpha}=0. $$

#### Proof.

The proof of this lemma is a simple adaptation of the argument from [21]. ∎

We now specify what we mean by the linearized Euler equations in velocity form. Take the unitary Fourier transform in $(x_{1},x_{3})$ , with frequencies $(k,\ell)$ , and let

$$ \mathcal{H}_{k,\ell}=\{V\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{y};\mathbb{C}^{3}):ikV_{1}+\partial_{y}V_{2}+i\ell V_{3}=0\}. $$

Let $\mathbb{P}_{k,\ell}$ be the orthogonal projection onto this space. Define the bounded operators

$$ L(k,\ell)V=-\mathbb{P}_{k,\ell}\bigl(ikPV+P^{\prime}V_{2}e_{1}\bigr)\quad\hbox{on }\mathcal{H}_{k,\ell}. $$

The direct integral of the operators $L(k,l)$ defines $L$ on $L^{2}_{\sigma}(\mathbb{R}^{3};\mathbb{C}^{3})$ , with domain

$$ D(L)=\left\{v\in L^{2}_{\sigma}(\mathbb{R}^{3};\mathbb{C}^{3}):\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\|L(k,\ell)\widehat{v}(k,\ell,\cdot)\|_{2}^{2}\,dk\,d\ell<\infty\right\}. $$

This is a closed, densely defined realization of the three-dimensional Euler equations linearized about the Okamoto shear flow: $-\mathbb{P}(P\partial_{1}v+P^{\prime}v_{2}e_{1})$ . In fact, the domain above can easily be seen to be the maximal domain of the operator on $L^{2}$ . Define $L_{\beta}=\beta L$ on $D(L)$ for $\beta\neq 0$ .

#### Theorem 4.2.

For every $\beta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ , the velocity linearization $L_{\beta}$ around $\overline{U}_{\beta}=\beta D(x_{2}/2)e_{1}$ has a positive real point in its approximate spectrum on $L^{2}_{\sigma}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{C}^{3})$ . More precisely, for each $0<\alpha<\alpha_{0}$ ,

$$ |\beta|\alpha\gamma_{\alpha}\in\sigma_{\rm ap}(L_{\beta}), $$

where $\gamma_{\alpha}$ is furnished by Lemma 4.1.

#### Proof.

Fix a mode from Lemma 4.1 and write $\phi=\phi_{\alpha}$ , $c=i\gamma_{\alpha}$ , and $\lambda=-i\alpha c>0$ . At $(k,\ell)=(\alpha,0)$ set $V_{\alpha}=(\phi^{\prime},-i\alpha\phi,0)$ . The Rayleigh equation implies $L(\alpha,0)V_{\alpha}=\lambda V_{\alpha}$ . For completeness, the associated pressure is $p=-(P-c)\phi^{\prime}+P^{\prime}\phi$ ; differentiation and the Rayleigh equation give $p^{\prime}=-\alpha^{2}(P-c)\phi$ . These identities verify the two nonzero components of the velocity eigenvalue equation before projection. Near $(\alpha,0)$ set $V_{k,\ell}=(\phi^{\prime},-ik\phi,0)$ . Its divergence on each fiber is exactly zero. The projections $\mathbb{P}_{k,\ell}$ vary continuously in operator norm in this neighborhood: after Fourier transform in $y$ , their symbols are the orthogonal projections perpendicular to $(k,\eta,\ell)$ , and $k^{2}+\eta^{2}+\ell^{2}\geq\alpha^{2}/4>0$ there. The symbols and their $(k,\ell)$ derivatives are uniformly bounded in $\eta$ . It follows that

$$ \|(L(k,\ell)-\lambda)V_{k,\ell}\|_{L^{2}_{y}}\longrightarrow 0\quad\hbox{as }(k,\ell)\to(\alpha,0). $$

Choose $a\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ with support in the unit ball of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and with $\|a\|_{2}=1$ . Let

$$ a_{n}(k,\ell)=n\,a(n(k-\alpha),n\ell),\qquad\widehat{v}_{n}=N_{n}^{-1}a_{n}(k,\ell)V_{k,\ell}, $$

where $N_{n}$ is the constant that makes $\|v_{n}\|_{2}=1$ . This is the wave packet construction. Then $N_{n}\to\|V_{\alpha}\|_{2}>0$ . Each $v_{n}$ is divergence free and belongs to $D(L)$ since its horizontal frequencies are bounded and $\|L(k,\ell)\|\leq|k|\|P\|_{\infty}+\|P^{\prime}\|_{\infty}$ . Plancherel’s identity gives

$$ \|(L-\lambda)v_{n}\|_{2}^{2}=N_{n}^{-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|a_{n}(k,\ell)|^{2}\|(L(k,\ell)-\lambda)V_{k,\ell}\|_{2}^{2}\,dk\,d\ell\longrightarrow 0. $$

This proves $\lambda\in\sigma_{\rm ap}(L)$ . The analogous claim for $L_{\beta}$ follows easily. ∎

#### Remark 4.3.

We note that a similar analysis can be done for the other shear flows identified by Okamoto, they all appear to admit the existence of unstable parts of the spectrum that are approximate eigenvalues.

We note that, for analytic semigroups, even an approximate unstable eigenvalue guarantees the existence of a nontrivial trajectory backwards in time $t\to-\infty$ (see [22]), which would be sufficient for the non-uniqueness program, as we discussed in Section 2. Note that neither the linearization of the self-similar Navier-Stokes equation nor the linearization of the Euler equation gives rise to an analytic semigroup. In the example above, then, the primary barrier to proving non-uniqueness from the data $1/y$ appears to be making sense of the singular limit to the Navier-Stokes equations when the profile anisotropically decays. We plan to investigate this direction further.

## 5. Stability of the Oseen Vortex

We study individual angular modes of the two-dimensional Euler linearization in vorticity variables. Let $\overline{u}(x)=u(r)e_{\theta}$ be a smooth real vector field on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , and write

$$ \Omega(r)=\frac{u(r)}{r},\qquad\overline{\omega}(r)=u^{\prime}(r)+\frac{u(r)}{r}. $$

Assume that $\Omega$ is bounded and $\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)=O(r^{-3})$ as $r\to\infty$ . Smoothness of the planar field implies $\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)=O(r)$ at zero, so $r\overline{\omega}^{\prime}$ is bounded. For $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $|k|\geq 2$ , set $\mathcal{X}_{k}=L^{2}((0,\infty),r\,dr;\mathbb{C})$ and define

$$ (L_{k}g)(r)=-ik\Omega(r)g(r)+ik\frac{\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)}{r}f(r). $$

Here the streamfunction is

$$ f(r)=-\frac{1}{2|k|}\left[\begin{aligned} &r^{-|k|}\int_{0}^{r}s^{|k|+1}g(s)\,ds\\
&+r^{|k|}\int_{r}^{\infty}s^{1-|k|}g(s)\,ds\end{aligned}\right]. $$

Both integrals exist for $g\in\mathcal{X}_{k}$ by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. This fixes the stream function normalization and shows that $f$ satisfies $f^{\prime\prime}+f^{\prime}/r-k^{2}f/r^{2}=g$ . To see that $L_{k}$ is bounded on $\mathcal{X}_{k}$ , set $G(s)=e^{s}g(e^{s})$ and $F(s)=e^{-s}f(e^{s})$ . Then

$$ G=T_{k}F,\qquad T_{k}=\partial_{s}^{2}+2\partial_{s}+1-k^{2}. $$

The Fourier symbol of $T_{k}$ is $-\eta^{2}+2i\eta+1-k^{2}$ , which has no real zero for $|k|\geq 2$ , and its inverse maps $L^{2}(\mathbb{R})$ boundedly into $H^{2}(\mathbb{R})$ . The same decomposition into modes and logarithmic change of coordinates was employed in [6]. The Green formula above is the inverse that gives our stream function $f$ and equivalently $F$ . Indeed, writing $n=|k|$ , it gives

$$ F(s)=-\frac{1}{2n}\left[\int_{-\infty}^{s}e^{-(n+1)(s-t)}G(t)\,dt+\int_{s}^{\infty}e^{-(n-1)(t-s)}G(t)\,dt\right]. $$

Both one-sided kernels are integrable, so $F\in L^{2}$ ; the equation $T_{k}F=G$ and the Fourier multiplier then give $F\in H^{2}$ . Under the unitary map $g\mapsto G$ , the operator becomes

$$ G\longmapsto-ik\Omega(e^{s})G+ike^{s}\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(e^{s})T_{k}^{-1}G. $$

It is therefore a bounded operator, with domain all of $\mathcal{X}_{k}$ .

#### Theorem 5.1.

Let $\overline{u}=u(r)e_{\theta}$ be a smooth real vector field on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , with bounded $\Omega=u/r$ and $\overline{\omega}^{\prime}=O(r^{-3})$ at infinity, where $\overline{\omega}=u^{\prime}+u/r$ . Suppose either $\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)>0$ for every $r>0$ , or $\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)<0$ for every $r>0$ . Then, for each integer $|k|\geq 2$ ,

$$ \sigma_{\rm p}(L_{k})\subset i\mathbb{R}. $$

Here $\sigma_{\rm p}$ denotes point spectrum on $\mathcal{X}_{k}$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose $L_{k}g=\lambda g$ , where $g\in\mathcal{X}_{k}$ , $\lambda=a+ib$ , and $a\neq 0$ . Since $F=T_{k}^{-1}G\in H^{2}(\mathbb{R})\subset L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ , the eigenvalue equation gives

$$ g(r)=\frac{ik\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)}{\lambda+ik\Omega(r)}F(\log r),\qquad|g(r)|\leq\frac{|k|}{|a|}\|F\|_{\infty}|\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)|. $$

In particular, $g(r)=O(r^{-3})$ at infinity. Writing $n=|k|\geq 2$ , the two terms in the Green formula satisfy

$$ r^{-n}\int_{0}^{r}s^{n+1}g(s)\,ds=O(r^{-1}),\qquad r^{n}\int_{r}^{\infty}s^{1-n}g(s)\,ds=O(r^{-1})\quad(r\to\infty). $$

For the first estimate split the integral at one; its tail is bounded by a constant times $\int_{1}^{r}s^{n-2}\,ds$ . Hence $f(r)=O(r^{-1})$ at infinity. At zero the boundedness of $F$ gives $f(r)=O(r)$ . Consequently $h(s)=f(e^{s})$ belongs to $L^{2}(\mathbb{R})$ . The eigenvalue equation and the streamfunction equation imply

$$ h^{\prime\prime}-k^{2}h=Q_{\lambda,k}h,\qquad Q_{\lambda,k}(s)=\frac{ike^{s}\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(e^{s})}{\lambda+ik\Omega(e^{s})}. $$

This coefficient is bounded, since $|\lambda+ik\Omega|\geq|a|$ . Therefore $h^{\prime\prime}\in L^{2}$ distributionally and $h\in H^{2}(\mathbb{R})$ . Integration by parts is now justified and gives

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}(|h^{\prime}|^{2}+k^{2}|h|^{2})\,ds=-\int_{\mathbb{R}}Q_{\lambda,k}|h|^{2}\,ds. $$

But

$$ \operatorname{Im}Q_{\lambda,k}(s)=\frac{kae^{s}\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(e^{s})}{a^{2}+(b+k\Omega(e^{s}))^{2}} $$

has a strict sign on $\mathbb{R}$ . Taking imaginary parts forces $h=0$ , and hence $f=g=0$ . Thus no eigenvalue has nonzero real part. ∎

For the radial mode $k=0$ , set $\mathcal{X}_{0}=L^{2}((0,\infty),r\,dr;\mathbb{C})$ and define $L_{0}=0$ on $\mathcal{X}_{0}$ . This agrees with the Euler linearization since a radial perturbation has tangential induced velocity, so both vorticity transport terms vanish. The modes $k=\pm 1$ are outside the scope of our theorem.

#### Corollary 5.2.

For the Oseen vortex

$$ \overline{u}(r,\theta)=\frac{1-e^{-r^{2}/4}}{r}e_{\theta},\qquad\overline{\omega}(r)=\frac{1}{2}e^{-r^{2}/4}, $$

the operators $L_{k}$ just defined satisfy $\sigma_{\rm p}(L_{k})\subset i\mathbb{R}$ for every integer $|k|\geq 2$ , and $L_{0}=0$ .

#### Proof.

The vector field extends smoothly through the origin, $\Omega(r)=(1-e^{-r^{2}/4})/r^{2}$ is bounded, and $\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)=-re^{-r^{2}/4}/4<0$ for $r>0$ . The hypotheses of Theorem 5.1 hold. ∎

#### Corollary 5.3.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.1, the linearization of the Euler equations in vorticity form around the Oseen vortex on the space

$$ L^{2}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{C}):=\{g\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{C}):g(-x)=g(x)\} $$

generates a strongly continuous group and satisfies $\sigma(L)\subset i\mathbb{R}$ and $s(L)=\omega_{0}(L)=0$ . In particular, this proves Theorem 1.6.

#### Proof.

We use the angular decomposition into even modes and the logarithmic change of coordinates from above. Put

$$ q(s)=e^{s}\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(e^{s}),\qquad A_{k}=-ik\Omega(e^{s}),\qquad B_{k}=ikqT_{k}^{-1}\quad(k\in 2\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}), $$

and set $A_{0}=B_{0}=0$ . Define $A=\bigoplus A_{k}$ on its maximal multiplication domain

$$ D(A)=\left\{(G_{k})\in\bigoplus_{k\in 2\mathbb{Z}}L^{2}(\mathbb{R}):\sum_{k}\|k\Omega(e^{s})G_{k}\|_{2}^{2}<\infty\right\}, $$

and $L=A+B$ on $D(A)$ , where $B=\bigoplus B_{k}$ . The operator $A$ is skew-adjoint. Since $q\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R})$ , the compactness from the Sobolev embedding and a cutoff approximation make each $B_{k}$ compact. Moreover, the symbol of $T_{k}$ gives

$$ \|B_{k}\|\leq\frac{|k|\|q\|_{\infty}}{k^{2}-1}\longrightarrow 0. $$

Thus $B$ is compact on $L^{2}$ , and the bounded perturbation theorem gives the strongly continuous group generated by $L$ .

For $\operatorname{Re}z\neq 0$ , compact perturbation of $A$ makes $z-L$ Fredholm of index zero. A nonzero vector in its kernel would have a nonzero angular component contradicting Theorem 5.1. Note also that the radial component satisfies $L_{0}=0$ . Hence $\sigma(L)\subset i\mathbb{R}$ , and $0\in\sigma(L)$ because the radial subspace is in the kernel.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$ . For all sufficiently large $|k|$ , $\|B_{k}\|\leq\varepsilon/2$ , so the Neumann series gives

$$ \sup_{\operatorname{Re}z\geq\varepsilon}\|(z-L_{k})^{-1}\|\leq 2/\varepsilon. $$

Each of the remaining finitely many $L_{k}$ is a bounded operator and has spectrum on the imaginary axis, so its resolvent is bounded on that half-plane, using continuity on bounded sets and its Neumann expansion at infinity. The direct-sum resolvent is therefore uniformly bounded there. The Gearhart–Prüss theorem [11, Theorem V.1.11] gives $\|e^{tL}\|\leq M_{\varepsilon}e^{\varepsilon t}$ for $t\geq 0$ . Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary and $0\in\sigma(L)$ , $\omega_{0}(L)=s(L)=0$ . ∎
